author: Dana DiFilippo
title: Democratic socialist says wins in Jersey City are a 'watershed' for far-left movement - NewsBreak
text:
By Dana DiFilippo ,
7 hours ago Joel Brooks, above, and Jake Ephros were elected on Dec. 2 to seats on Jersey City's council. (Photos by Fran Baltzer and Roman Broszkowski)
It might seem like democratic socialism is having its moment in the sun, with two of the movement’s members snagging council seats in Jersey City’s runoff election Tuesday just a month after Zohran Mamdani’s victory in the New York City mayoral race.
Supporters say the wins — marking the first time a democratic socialist has been elected to public office in New Jersey in over a century — represent more than a moment. They signal a trend. And many in the movement, which rejects capitalism in favor of community ownership, have their eyes set on higher office.
“This is watershed for us, absolutely,” said Jake Ephros, who was elected to Jersey City’s council along with fellow democratic socialist Joel Brooks.
The movement’s activists have worked for years to build a bench of electable democratic socialist candidates, relying on labor unions to help grow grassroots support and taking lessons from prominent politicians who identify as democratic socialists including Reps. Alexandria O’Casio Cortez (D-NY) and Rashida Talib (D-MI), a national organizer said.
But the growing resentments of the working class, backlash against corporate-funded Democratic incumbents, and frustration with President Donald Trump’s policies coalesced to ensure a banner year for the Democratic Socialists of America, said Chanpreet Singh, a national electoral organizer with the group.
Voters elected more than half of the 21 democratic socialist candidates the group endorsed and funded across the country this year, including Ephros and Brooks, Singh said.
The group’s fundraising slogan: “Socialist cash takes out capitalist trash.”
Jersey City Councilman-elect Jake Ephros celebrating his election victory in Jersey City on Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Roman Broszkowski) “There is a lot of exasperation with the establishment, with the way things are going, just business as usual,” Singh said. “Candidates like Jake and Joel, they championed really bold, unapologetically socialist policies, like universal rent control and child care. These are things that speak to people in a moment when they’re feeling really frustrated, the cost of living is rising, and they want something more than what your typical Democratic incumbent offers.”
The group hopes to get more democratic socialists elected to Congress in coming years, Singh added.
Dan Cassino is a professor of government and law at Fairleigh Dickinson University and the executive director of the school’s poll. He agreed socialism has largely lost the stigma, at least among progressives, that it historically has carried due to its association with authoritarianism.
“In urban areas of New York and New Jersey, socialism just isn’t the bugbear that it used to be,” Cassino said.
While the proportion of New Jersey Democrats who identify as socialists has remained around 10 percent in recent years, even voters who don’t consider themselves socialists are willing to vote for a candidate who is, Cassino said. For Democratic candidates, being an avowed democratic socialist can give them an edge with Democrats who have become alienated from the institutional party, he added.
Still, Cassino noted, political ideology tends to matter less to voters than policy priorities and campaign promises.
“These candidates are running almost more as technocrats than anything else. They’re identifying problems, especially with regard to affordability, and offering what seems to voters to be reasonable solutions to those problems,” Cassino said. “At the end of the day, people want to hear that candidates understand the problems they’re facing, and have a solution. Ideological labels don’t matter as much as a belief that they can solve real problems.”
Ephros and Brooks both ran on platforms focused on affordability and quality-of-life issues, calling for more state funding for schools, the creation of a municipal transit council to improve mass transit, and more investment in public health care, among other things.
Brooks, a labor organizer who will represent Jersey City’s west side, also ran for city council in 2021 but fell short by about 200 votes. He did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
Ephros, a teacher and union organizer who will represent the city’s northern neighborhoods, told the New Jersey Monitor that his first priorities, once he’s sworn in next month, will be to enact universal rent control, tackle trash issues including making collection a municipal function instead of privatized, and enforce existing laws to hold absentee landlords accountable for property problems.
Ephros credited his election success partly to the same voter frustrations Singh mentioned, adding that working people overburdened by the ever-climbing cost of living were hungry for change.
And while widespread frustration with Trump’s policies united Democrats and mobilized them to the polls, Ephros thinks his and Brooks’ solutions-focused platforms and can-do attitudes made the difference at the ballot box.
“We can’t only fight against something. We have to be fighting for something. And so we aren’t only saying: ‘Vote for me. I’m going to fight Trump!’ It’s: ‘We’re going to pick up the trash. We’re going to get our streets paved. We’re going to cap our rents. We’re going to fight back against the tax breaks that we’ve been giving billionaire developers on the backs of ordinary homeowners,’” Ephros said. “We’re going to do all of these concrete, tangible, and positive things to make life better for ordinary people here — with their help, not for them, but with them.”
